Logistic regression has 2 components 1. Link function: Map outcome to predictors without breaking the boundary rules (0 to 1) 2. Inverse link function: Map predictors to outcome to turn a mathematical score into real-world predictions

+----------+------------------+---------------+---------------+------------------+
| Model    | Random component | Bound by      | Link function | Inverse link     |
+==========+==================+===============+===============+==================+
| Logistic | Binomial (1/0)   | P e (1, 0)    | Logit link    | Sigmoid function |
|          |                  |               |               |                  |
|          |                  |               | ln(p/(1-p))   |                  |
+----------+------------------+---------------+---------------+------------------+
| Poisson  | POisson          | (0, infinity) | Log link      | .....            |
|          |                  |               |               |                  |
|          |                  |               | log(miu)      |                  |
+----------+------------------+---------------+---------------+------------------+

The logistic regression model creates beta values based on the log-odds, ln(p/(1-p)).

- we need to convert back to readable coefficients

# Geographic cross-validation

Random k-folds vs Leave One District Out

- k-folds: will be random stuff. but due to spatial autocorrelation, will create spatial leakage where you know stuff about nearby cells –\> will get inflated sense of how well the model will do on truly unseen data, bc of the sptial spillover effect

- LODO –\> comes up with geographically segmented training and testing dataset –\> won't have spatial spillover effect.

# Odds vs Probability

- Odds: How many more times likely is it to happen than it doesn't?

  - $p/(1-p)$

  - if p = 0.5 (50% chance of happening), odds = 1. Outcome is 1x more likely to happen than it doesn't –\> even odds

  - p = 0.5 and odds = 1 is the baseline

  - p \< 0.5, odds \< 1 (positive number)

  - p \> 0.5, odds \> 1

probability –\> odds –\> log-odds –\> needed to make linear prediction

\$log(p/(1-p)) = beta + betax + betax2.... \$

- then solve for p –\> creates a sigmoid function

Output of logistic regression

- 1 log-odds

- odds ratio (if odds ratio \> 1, p \> 0.5)
